claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal-based HEA nanomaterials is governed by the balance between nucleation kinetics and surface diffusion during synthesis.
Catalytic performance of noble metal-based HEA nanomaterials is governed by the balance between nucleation kinetics and surface diffusion during synthesis.
Slower precursor delivery promotes uniform atomic mixing.
Slower precursor delivery promotes formation of a homogeneous disordered solid-solution phase.
A homogeneous disordered solid solution maximizes cocktail and strain effects.
Cocktail and strain effects expose optimized adsorption sites for catalytic reactions.
The controlled comparison uses a slow precursor-injection rate of approximately 0.6 mL/hr and a fast rate of approximately 1.5 mL/hr.
The targeted structural mediator is an approximately equiatomic FCC disordered solid solution.
The targeted solid solution has uniform elemental distribution and minimal phase segregation.
Slight lattice distortions induce strain and electronic modulation at the exposed surface.
Slower precursor injection suppresses rapid nucleation events that would otherwise produce metal-rich clusters.
Enhanced surface diffusion under slow-injection conditions enables uniform incorporation of all constituent metals.
Uniform incorporation maximizes the cocktail effect and strain-induced orbital hybridization.
Cocktail effects and strain-induced orbital hybridization tune adsorption energies of catalytic intermediates.
Tuned adsorption energies improve catalytic activity and durability.
Slow-injection catalysts will have a more uniform atomic distribution than fast-injection catalysts.
Slow-injection catalysts will exhibit lower overpotential and higher current density than fast-injection catalysts.
Slow-injection catalysts will exhibit greater electrochemical durability than fast-injection catalysts.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for wet-chemical synthesis below 250°C and catalytic operation below 80°C in acidic or alkaline electrolyte.
Failure of slow injection to improve both atomic homogeneity and catalytic performance relative to the fast-injection control, or detection of phase segregation, would falsify the hypothesis.
